abstract: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are major risk factors for heart failure, and impaired fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is a key contributor to metabolic dysfunction in obesity-related cardiomyopathy. However, how the heart maintains FAO and adapts to chronic lipid overload remains poorly understood. Here, we identify SET and MYND domain-containing protein 1 (Smyd1), a muscle-specific histone methyltransferase, as an early compensatory regulator of cardiac metabolism in response to lipid overload. In wild-type mouse hearts, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding induced transient increases in Smyd1 expression and H3K4me3 levels during the early-to-mid phase of metabolic stress, both of which returned to baseline levels during prolonged HFD exposure. Single-cell RNA sequencing further revealed that this adaptive increase in Smyd1 expression occurred predominantly in cardiomyocytes. In contrast, cardiac-specific Smyd1 heterozygous knockout mice exhibited accelerated cardiac dysfunction, left ventricular dilation, increased myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival following HFD feeding. Mechanistically, Smyd1 deficiency impaired the adaptive upregulation of key FAO-related genes and reduced cardiac FAO activity. Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation analysis revealed an interaction between Smyd1 and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR), suggesting a potential mechanism by which Smyd1 supports FAO gene expression. Taken together, these findings identify Smyd1 as an early compensatory regulator that supports FAO-dependent metabolic adaptation and protects the heart against lipid overload-induced cardiac dysfunction. This adaptive mechanism, involving H3K4me3 regulation and the Smyd1-PPAR interaction, may provide potential therapeutic targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving cardiac metabolic flexibility in obesity-related cardiomyopathy.
